results.title: The tripling sequence of Ramanujan's Entry 6
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For natural numbers $n$ and $k$, let $A(n, k) = 3^k n + (3^k - 1)/2$, a natural number. It is the sequence with $A(n, 0) = n$ and $A(n, k + 1) = 3A(n, k) + 1$.

results.title: Starting value of the tripling sequence
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $n$, the tripling sequence $A(n, k)$ of Entry 6 satisfies $A(n, 0) = n$.

results.title: Recurrence of the tripling sequence
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For all natural numbers $n$ and $k$, the tripling sequence $A(n, k)$ of Entry 6 satisfies $A(n, k + 1) = 3A(n, k) + 1$.

results.title: The tripling sequence never drops below its starting value
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For all natural numbers $n$ and $k$, the tripling sequence $A(n, k)$ of Entry 6 satisfies $n \le A(n, k)$.

results.title: Supersingular elliptic curves
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $p$ be a prime and let $E$ be an elliptic curve over an algebraic closure $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p$ of $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$. Then $E$ is called supersingular when every point $P \in E(\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p)$ with $pP = 0$ is $P = 0$.

results.title: Supersingularity from trivial prime-power torsion
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $p$ be a prime and let $E$ be an elliptic curve over an algebraic closure $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p$ of $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$. If for every integer $r \ge 1$ the only point $P \in E(\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p)$ with $p^r P = 0$ is $P = 0$, then $E$ is supersingular.

results.title: Supersingular curves have trivial prime-power torsion
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $p$ be a prime and let $E$ be a supersingular elliptic curve over an algebraic closure $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p$ of $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$. Then for every integer $r \ge 1$, every point $P \in E(\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p)$ with $p^r P = 0$ is $P = 0$.

results.title: Stability of the determinant polynomial
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every finite family $A_1, \dots, A_m$ of positive semidefinite complex square matrices whose rows and columns are indexed by a finite set $d$, the polynomial $\det\left(x I + \sum_{i=1}^m z_i A_i\right)$ in the variables $x, z_1, \dots, z_m$, where $I$ is the identity matrix, is stable.

results.title: Real stability of the determinant polynomial
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every finite family $A_1, \dots, A_m$ of positive semidefinite complex square matrices whose rows and columns are indexed by a finite set $d$, the polynomial $\det\left(x I + \sum_{i=1}^m z_i A_i\right)$ in the variables $x, z_1, \dots, z_m$, where $I$ is the identity matrix, is real stable.

results.title: Degree of a mixed characteristic polynomial
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every finite family $A_1, \dots, A_m$ of complex square matrices whose rows and columns are indexed by a finite set $d$, the mixed characteristic polynomial of $A_1, \dots, A_m$ has degree $|d|$, the number of elements of $d$.

results.title: Mixed characteristic polynomials of positive semidefinite matrices are real-rooted

Then the largest real part of a root of the mixed characteristic polynomial of $A_1, \dots, A_m$ is at most $(1 + \sqrt{\eta})^2$.

results.title: Cubic family
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a parameter $\lambda \in \mathbb{C}$, the cubic polynomial map $f_\lambda : \mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{C}$ is given by $f_\lambda(z) = \lambda z^2 + z^3$.

results.title: Critical points of the cubic family
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For $\lambda \in \mathbb{C}$, a point $c \in \mathbb{C}$ is a critical point of $f_\lambda(z) = \lambda z^2 + z^3$ when $f_\lambda$ has complex derivative $0$ at $c$, that is, $f_\lambda'(c) = 0$.

results.title: Basin of attraction of zero
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For $\lambda \in \mathbb{C}$, the basin of zero of $f_\lambda(z) = \lambda z^2 + z^3$ is the set of $z \in \mathbb{C}$ whose forward orbit tends to $0$, that is, $f_\lambda^{n}(z) \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$, where $f_\lambda^{n}$ denotes the $n$-th iterate of $f_\lambda$.

results.title: Immediate basin of zero
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For $\lambda \in \mathbb{C}$, a set $V \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ is the immediate basin of zero of $f_\lambda(z) = \lambda z^2 + z^3$ when $0 \in V$, $V$ is contained in the basin of zero of $f_\lambda$ (the set of $z$ with $f_\lambda^{n}(z) \to 0$), $V$ is connected, and every connected set $W \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ with $0 \in W$ that is contained in the basin of zero of $f_\lambda$ satisfies $W \subseteq V$. Thus $V$…

results.title: Parameters with both critical points in the immediate basin
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The parameter set is the set of $\lambda \in \mathbb{C}$ for which some immediate basin of zero $V$ of $f_\lambda(z) = \lambda z^2 + z^3$ contains every critical point of $f_\lambda$.

results.title: Parameter components
results.caption: Definition

results.title: Jordan curves in the plane
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A set $S \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ is a Jordan curve when there is a continuous injective map $f$ from the unit circle $\{z \in \mathbb{C} : |z| = 1\}$ to $\mathbb{C}$ whose image is exactly $S$.

results.title: McMullen's question on Jordan boundaries of cubic parameter components
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $f_\lambda(z) = \lambda z^2 + z^3$ for $\lambda \in \mathbb{C}$. The statement is that for every parameter component $U$, that is, every connected component of the set of $\lambda$ for which every critical point of $f_\lambda$ lies in the immediate basin of zero of $f_\lambda$, the boundary $\partial U$ of $U$ in $\mathbb{C}$ is a Jordan curve.

results.title: Roesch's theorem on the boundaries of cubic parameter components
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For the cubic family $f_\lambda(z) = \lambda z^2 + z^3$ with $\lambda \in \mathbb{C}$, the boundary of every parameter component is a Jordan curve. Here a parameter component is a connected component of the set of $\lambda$ for which every critical point of $f_\lambda$ lies in the immediate basin of zero of $f_\lambda$.

results.title: The standard cube in $\mathbb{F}_3^n$
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the standard cube is the set $\{0, 1\}^n \subseteq \mathbb{F}_3^n$ of vectors each of whose coordinates is $0$ or $1$.

results.title: Cubes in $\mathbb{F}_3^n$
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A set $A \subseteq \mathbb{F}_3^n$ is a cube if there is an $\mathbb{F}_3$-linear automorphism $e$ of $\mathbb{F}_3^n$ with $A = e(\{0, 1\}^n)$, the image of the standard cube $\{0, 1\}^n$ under $e$.

results.title: A sumset of $100$ sets equal to $\mathbb{F}_3^n$
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For sets $A_1, \dots, A_{100} \subseteq \mathbb{F}_3^n$, the property that every $v \in \mathbb{F}_3^n$ can be written as $v = a_1 + \dots + a_{100}$ with $a_i \in A_i$ for each $i$, that is, $A_1 + \dots + A_{100} = \mathbb{F}_3^n$.

results.title: Cook–Levin theorem: SAT is NP-complete
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let SAT be the decision problem on bitstrings that accepts exactly the encodings of satisfiable CNF formulas. Then SAT belongs to NP, and every decision problem $L$ in NP is polynomial-time many-one reducible to SAT: there is a function $f$ from bitstrings to bitstrings, computable in polynomial time, such that $L(x) = \mathrm{SAT}(f(x))$ for every bitstring $x$.

uses: The classes P, NP and coNP

results.title: NOT-ALL-EQUAL 3-SAT instances
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: A NOT-ALL-EQUAL 3-SAT instance is a pair $(n, \varphi)$ of a natural number $n$, the number of variables, and a CNF formula $\varphi$. The formula is not required to have three literals per clause; that is part of well-formedness.

results.title: Well-formed NOT-ALL-EQUAL 3-SAT instances
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A NOT-ALL-EQUAL 3-SAT instance $(n, \varphi)$ is well-formed when every clause of $\varphi$ is a list of exactly three literals, repetitions allowed, and every literal $(x, b)$ in it has variable index $x < n$.

results.title: Not-all-equal satisfiability of an instance
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A NOT-ALL-EQUAL 3-SAT instance $(n, \varphi)$, with $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and $\varphi$ a CNF formula, is not-all-equal satisfiable when there are truth values $a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ such that, for the assignment $v$ with $v(x) = a_x$ for $x < n$ and $v(x) = \mathrm{false}$ for $x \ge n$, every clause of $\varphi$ contains a literal satisfied by $v$ and a literal not satisfied by $v$.

results.title: NOT-ALL-EQUAL 3-SAT as a decision problem
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The decision problem NOT-ALL-EQUAL 3-SAT accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding, to a NOT-ALL-EQUAL 3-SAT instance $(n, \varphi)$ that is well-formed and not-all-equal satisfiable. Every bitstring that decodes to no instance is rejected.

results.title: NOT-ALL-EQUAL 3-SAT is NP-complete
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The decision problem NOT-ALL-EQUAL 3-SAT over bitstrings belongs to NP, and every decision problem in NP has a polynomial-time many-one reduction to it.

results.title: Skip-list node
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: A skip-list node consists of a key, a value and a natural number, the height of its tower. The node itself does not require the height to be positive; positivity is part of the validity invariant of skip lists.

results.title: Skip list
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: A deterministic skip list with keys in $\alpha$ and values in $\beta$ is represented by the list of its bottom-level nodes, each node an entry carrying a key in $\alpha$, a value in $\beta$ and a tower height, a natural number. No ordering or height condition is imposed by this structure.

results.title: Empty skip list
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The empty skip list is the skip list with no nodes.

results.title: Valid skip list
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type. A skip list with keys in $\alpha$ and values in $\beta$ is valid when the keys of its bottom-level nodes are strictly increasing along the list and every node has a tower of positive height.

results.title: Level of a skip list
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a skip list and a level index $i$ (levels are numbered from $0$ at the bottom), level $i$ is the list of key-value pairs $(k, v)$ of the stored nodes whose tower height $h$ satisfies $i < h$, in the order in which these nodes appear in the bottom-level list of the skip list.

results.title: Bottom-level abstraction of a skip list
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The bottom-level abstraction of a skip list is the association list obtained from its bottom-level nodes, in order, by keeping the key-value pair $(k, v)$ of each node and forgetting its tower height.

results.title: Stored tower height of a key
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a key $k$ and a skip list $S$, the stored tower height of $k$ in $S$ is the tower height of the first bottom-level node of $S$ whose key equals $k$ under the given Boolean equality test on keys; it is undefined when no node has key $k$.

results.title: One level of skip-list search
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $k$ be a search key, $i$ a zero-based level and $L$ a list of skip-list nodes. Let $P$ be the longest prefix of $L$ whose nodes all have keys less than $k$. If some node of $P$ has tower height greater than $i$ (so it is visible at level $i$), advancing at level $i$ returns the part of $L$ after the last such node; otherwise it returns $L$ unchanged.

results.title: Skip-list search window
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $k$ be a key and let $H$ be the greatest tower height in a skip list ($H = 0$ if the list is empty or every tower has height $0$). Start with the full list of bottom-level nodes, and for each level $i$ from $H - 1$ down to $0$ in turn (no levels when $H = 0$) replace the current list by the result of advancing at level $i$: within the longest initial segment of the current list whose keys are all less than $k$,…

results.title: Skip-list lookup
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The lookup of a key $k$ in a skip list computes the search window for $k$, the suffix of the bottom-level nodes reached by descending from the highest level to level $0$, and returns the value of the first node in the window whose key is $k$, or no value if the window has no such node.

results.title: Skip-list insertion
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: To insert key $k$ with value $v$ and requested height $h$ into a skip list, scan its bottom-level nodes in order, keeping every node whose key is less than $k$. At the first node whose key is not less than $k$: if its key equals $k$, its value is replaced by $v$ and its tower height is kept; if its key is greater than $k$, a new node with key $k$, value $v$ and tower height $\max(1, h)$ is placed before it. If…

results.title: The empty skip list is valid
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every linearly ordered type $\alpha$ and every type $\beta$, the empty skip list with keys in $\alpha$ and values in $\beta$ is valid.

results.title: Skip-list levels are sorted by key
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If a skip list is valid, then for every level index $i$ (levels are numbered from $0$ at the bottom), the keys in the list of key-value pairs visible at level $i$ are strictly increasing: every pair has a strictly smaller key than every pair after it.

results.title: Each skip-list level is a subsequence of the level below
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every skip list and every level index $i$ (levels are numbered from $0$ at the bottom), the list of key-value pairs visible at level $i + 1$ is a subsequence, not necessarily contiguous, of the list of key-value pairs visible at level $i$.

results.title: Keys of a valid skip list are distinct
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If a skip list is valid, then the keys of the pairs in its bottom-level abstraction, read in order, form a list without duplicates.

results.title: Keys on each skip-list level are distinct
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If a skip list is valid, then for every level index $i$ (levels are numbered from $0$ at the bottom), no key occurs twice in the list of key-value pairs visible at level $i$.

results.title: One search step returns a suffix
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every search key, every level $i$ and every list $L$ of skip-list nodes, advancing the search at level $i$ on $L$ returns a suffix of $L$.

results.title: The search window is a suffix of the bottom level
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every skip list and every key $k$, the search window for $k$ is a suffix of the list of the skip list's bottom-level nodes.

results.title: Skip-list search agrees with bottom-level lookup
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every skip list and every key $k$, the top-down skip-list lookup of $k$ returns the same result as looking up $k$ in the bottom-level abstraction, the list of key-value pairs of all stored nodes in order: the value of the first pair with key $k$, or no value if there is none.

results.title: Insertion preserves skip-list validity
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type and $\beta$ a type. If a skip list with keys in $\alpha$ and values in $\beta$ is valid, then for every key $k \in \alpha$, value $v \in \beta$ and requested height $h \in \mathbb{N}$ (including $h = 0$), inserting $k$ with value $v$ and requested height $h$ yields a valid skip list. This covers both a new key and a key already present, whose value is replaced.

results.title: Lookup after insertion returns the inserted value
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every skip list, key $k$, value $v$ and requested height $h$, looking up $k$ after inserting $k$ with value $v$ and requested height $h$ returns $v$.

results.title: Skip-list insertion does not change lookup of other keys
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type. For every skip list $S$ with keys in $\alpha$ and values in $\beta$, all keys $k$ and $k'$ in $\alpha$ with $k' \ne k$, every value $v \in \beta$ and every requested height $h \in \mathbb{N}$, looking up $k'$ in the skip list obtained by inserting $k$ with value $v$ and requested height $h$ into $S$ gives the same result as looking up $k'$ in $S$.

results.title: Reinsertion preserves tower height
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $S$ be a valid skip list in which the key $k$ has stored tower height $h_0$. Then after inserting $k$ into $S$ with any value and any requested height, the stored tower height of $k$ is still $h_0$.

results.title: Height of a newly inserted key
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If a key $k$ does not occur in a skip list $S$, then after inserting $k$ into $S$ with any value and requested height $h$, the stored tower height of $k$ is $\max(1, h)$.

results.title: Skip-list erasure
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given a key $k$ from a linearly ordered type and a skip list $S$, the erasure of $k$ from $S$ is the skip list obtained by scanning the entries of $S$ in order: an entry whose key is less than $k$ is kept and the scan continues; at the first entry whose key is greater than $k$ the scan stops, and that entry and all later ones are kept; at the first entry whose key equals $k$ that entry is removed, the scan stops,…

results.title: Erasing from the empty skip list
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every key $k$, erasing $k$ from the empty skip list gives the empty skip list.

results.title: Erasing a key below the first entry
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $e$ be a skip-list entry and $L$ a list of entries. If a key $k$ is less than the key of $e$, then erasing $k$ from the skip list with entry list $e$ followed by $L$ leaves the entry list $e$ followed by $L$ unchanged.

results.title: Erasing past a smaller first entry
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $e$ be a skip-list entry and $L$ a list of entries. If the key of $e$ is less than a key $k$, then erasing $k$ from the skip list with entry list $e$ followed by $L$ gives the entry list consisting of $e$ followed by the entry list obtained by erasing $k$ from the skip list with entry list $L$.

results.title: Erasing the key of the first entry
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $e$ be a skip-list entry and $L$ a list of entries, and consider the skip list whose entry list is $e$ followed by $L$. If a key $k$ equals the key of $e$, then erasing $k$ from this skip list leaves the entry list $L$.

results.title: Erasure on a valid skip list filters out the key
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $S$ is a valid skip list and $k$ is a key, then the entry list of the skip list obtained by erasing $k$ from $S$ is the entry list of $S$ with every entry whose key equals $k$ removed, the remaining entries kept in their order.

results.title: Erasure preserves skip-list validity
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $L$ be a valid skip list, that is, its keys are strictly increasing and every stored tower has positive height. For every key $k$, the skip list obtained from $L$ by erasing $k$ is again valid.

results.title: Erased keys are absent from a skip list
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $L$ be a valid skip list, that is, its keys are strictly increasing and every stored tower has positive height. For every key $k$, looking up $k$ in the skip list obtained from $L$ by erasing $k$ returns no value.

results.title: Erasure preserves lookups of other keys
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $S$ is a valid skip list and $k$, $k'$ are keys with $k' \ne k$, then looking up $k'$ in the skip list obtained by erasing $k$ from $S$ gives the same result as looking up $k'$ in $S$: the same value, or no value in both.

results.title: The erased key has no stored height
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $S$ is a valid skip list and $k$ is a key, then after erasing $k$ from $S$ the key $k$ has no stored tower height.

results.title: Erasure preserves the heights of other keys
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $S$ is a valid skip list and $k$, $k'$ are keys with $k' \ne k$, then the stored tower height of $k'$ in the skip list obtained by erasing $k$ from $S$ is the same as in $S$; in particular $k'$ has no stored height in one exactly when it has none in the other.

results.title: Erasure removes the key from every level
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $S$ is a valid skip list, $k$ is a key and $i$ is a natural number, then the level-$i$ list of key-value pairs (levels numbered from $0$) of the skip list obtained by erasing $k$ from $S$ is the level-$i$ list of $S$ with every pair whose key equals $k$ removed, the remaining pairs kept in their order.

results.title: Z-algorithm
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given a word $s = s_0 \dots s_{n-1}$ over a type $\alpha$ with a Boolean equality test, Gusfield's Z-box algorithm returns an array $Z$ of $n$ natural numbers with $Z_0 = n$. It visits $i = 1, \dots, n - 1$ in turn, keeping a box $[\ell, r)$, initially empty, that is the rightmost match of a prefix of $s$ found so far. If $\ell \le i < r$ and $Z_{i - \ell} < r - i$, it sets $Z_i = Z_{i - \ell}$. Otherwise it finds…

results.title: The first Z-value is the word length
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type with a Boolean equality test. For every nonempty word of length $n$ over $\alpha$, the Z-array $Z$ computed by the Z-algorithm has $Z_0 = n$.

results.title: Z-values are longest common prefix lengths
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type with a lawful Boolean equality test, let $s = s_0 \dots s_{n-1}$ be a word over $\alpha$, and let $Z$ be the Z-array computed by the Z-algorithm on $s$. For every position $i < n$ and every natural number $q$, $q \le Z_i$ holds if and only if $q \le n - i$ and $s_k = s_{i+k}$ for all $k < q$. Hence $Z_i$ is the length of the longest common prefix of $s$ and its suffix $s_i \dots s_{n-1}$.

results.title: Z-values are at most the suffix length
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type with a Boolean equality test, not necessarily lawful, and let $s$ be a word of length $n$ over $\alpha$. For every position $i < n$, the entry at $i$ of the Z-array computed by the Z-algorithm on $s$ is at most $n - i$.

results.title: Linear upper bound for the Z-algorithm
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type with a Boolean equality test, not necessarily lawful. On every word of length $n$ over $\alpha$, the Z-algorithm has cost at most $3(n - 1)$, read as $0$ when $n = 0$, where the cost counts one unit for each visited position $i \ge 1$ and one unit for each symbol comparison.

results.title: Linear lower bound for the Z-algorithm
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type with a Boolean equality test, not necessarily lawful. On every word of length $n$ over $\alpha$, the Z-algorithm has cost at least $n - 1$, where the cost counts one unit for each visited position $i \ge 1$ and one unit for each symbol comparison.

results.title: Z-array of a repeated symbol
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type with a lawful Boolean equality test, let $a \in \alpha$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$. The Z-array computed by the Z-algorithm on the word $a^n$ has entry $n - i$ at every position $i < n$.

results.title: Z-algorithm cost on a repeated symbol
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type with a lawful Boolean equality test, let $a \in \alpha$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$. The Z-algorithm run on the word $a^n$ has cost exactly $2(n - 1)$, read as $0$ when $n = 0$, where the cost counts one unit for each visited position $i \ge 1$ and one unit for each symbol comparison. Thus it makes $n - 1$ visits and $n - 1$ comparisons.

results.title: Z-algorithm cost on a repeated symbol followed by a distinct one
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type with a lawful Boolean equality test and let $a \ne b$ be elements of $\alpha$. For every $n \ge 1$, the Z-algorithm run on the word $a^n b$ has cost exactly $3n - 1$, where the cost counts one unit for each visited position $i \ge 1$ and one unit for each symbol comparison. In terms of the input length $N = n + 1$, this is $3N - 4$.
